summary.text: A cinder cone is a steep, cone-shaped hill of loose volcanic fragments, such as ash and scoria, piled up around a volcanic vent.
Gas-charged lava blasted into the air breaks into small pieces that harden and fall around the vent, building a cone that is often symmetrical with slopes of 30° to 40°.
Late in an eruption, gas-poor lava is denser than the cinders and too much for the weak, loose cone to hold, so it often breaks out along the base rather than the top.

facts.label: Size range
facts.value: Tens to hundreds of meters tall

facts.label: Most famous example
facts.value: Parícutin, which grew from a Mexican corn field in 1943

facts.label: Parícutin's final height
facts.value: 424 meters after nine years of eruptions

items.prompt: Near the end of a cinder cone eruption, molten rock that has lost most of its gas rises inside the cone. Where does it usually come out?

options.label: As a tall fountain from the summit crater
Along the bottom of the cone, lifting the cinders
Nowhere; it hardens deep inside the cone
Through a blast that flattens the whole cone

items.explain: The loose cinders are too weak to hold rising molten rock, and gas-poor lava is denser than the cinders, so it burrows out along the base and floats the cinders up like corks.

items.prompt: Pieces collected from a cinder cone are glassy and full of tiny frozen gas bubbles. What explains this?

options.label: Slow cooling deep underground over many years
Seawater soaking into the rock after it formed
Magma bursting into the air and cooling very fast
Lightning melting sand on the cone's surface

items.explain: Gas-charged magma is blown into the air in fragments that cool so quickly the bubbles are trapped in place, leaving glassy rock.

items.prompt: Imagine a cinder cone erupting on a world with weaker gravity and thinner air than Earth. How would it most likely differ from one on Earth?

options.label: Much wider, because fragments fly farther out
Much taller, because fragments stack more steeply
Identical, since only the magma decides its shape
Smaller, because thin air stops eruptions early

items.explain: Lower gravity and air pressure let ejected particles spread over a larger area; cinder cones on Mars seem more than twice as wide as those on Earth.

items.prompt: While a cinder cone is erupting, a strong wind blows steadily from the west for weeks. What shape does the cone likely take?

options.label: A perfectly even cone, since wind cannot move cinders
A cone with extra cinder piled on its west side
A flat sheet of lava with no cone at all
A lopsided cone with more cinder on its east side

items.explain: Cinder cones are often symmetrical, but strong prevailing winds pile more cinder on the downwind side of the vent, which here is the east.

items.prompt: In a volcanic field where magma arrives only rarely, each eruption tends to build its own new little cone in a new spot. Why?

options.label: Each old cone is fully sealed by thick ice
No lasting path to the surface stays open between eruptions
The magma is too thick to rise more than once
Earthquakes move the ground a long way each year

items.explain: With a very low magma supply spread out in space and time, no eruption sets up 'plumbing' for the next, so each must find its own way up.

items.prompt: A geologist studies a small volcanic cone built from large lava blobs that stuck together as they landed. Why would she not call it a cinder cone?

options.label: Cinder cones only form on the ocean floor
Cinder cones are always over a kilometer tall
Cinder cones are built of loose, unjoined fragments
Cinder cones never contain any basalt rock

items.explain: Cinder cones are made of loose cinder or scoria, which sets them apart from spatter cones built of clumped-together volcanic bombs.
